blocks.text: Branched-chain alkanes are named by the following rules.

items: Locate the longest continuous chain of carbon atoms; it determines the parent name. A compound whose longest chain has six carbons is a hexane even if the chain is bent; the longest chain may not be obvious from the way the formula is written, and a compound is a heptane if its longest chain has seven carbons.
Number the longest chain from the end nearest the substituent.
Use the numbers from rule 2 to give the location of the substituent: the parent name is placed last and the substituent, preceded by its number, first (for example 2-methylhexane).

With two or more substituents, give each a number for its position on the longest chain, for example 4-ethyl-2-methylhexane. List the substituents alphabetically (ethyl before methyl), ignoring multiplying prefixes such as di and tri.
When two substituents are on the same carbon atom, use that number twice.
When two or more substituents are identical, use the prefixes di, tri, tetra and so on, and make certain that every substituent has a number.
When two chains of equal length compete as the parent chain, choose the chain with the greater number of substituents.
When branching first occurs at an equal distance from either end of the longest chain, choose the name that gives the lower number at the first point of difference.

blocks.long_description: To name a branched alkane, find the longest chain, number it from the end nearer a branch, and list the substituents alphabetically with their positions, so a hexane chain with a methyl on carbon 2 and an ethyl on carbon 4 is 4-ethyl-2-methylhexane. Cycloalkanes take the prefix cyclo- and ring numbering that gives the lowest locants. Every alkane carbon is sp3 hybridised with four sigma bonds at 109.5 degrees, giving a tetrahedral shape and 1.54 angstrom carbon-carbon bonds, while cycloalkanes close those tetrahedra into rings. Alkanes up to four carbons are gases, five to seventeen liquids and eighteen upward waxy solids; boiling points rise with chain length and fall with branching.

blocks.prompt: Write the displayed formula of 2,3,3-trimethylhexane and name CH3C(CH3)2CH2CH(CH3)CH3 (Quick Check 11.1b; rules 6 and 8).
blocks.explanation: 2,3,3-Trimethylhexane: a six-carbon chain with one methyl on carbon 2 and two on carbon 3, CH3CH(CH3)C(CH3)2CH2CH2CH3. The second compound has a five-carbon chain with methyls on carbons 2, 2 and 4 from one end or 2, 4 and 4 from the other; the lower number at the first point of difference wins: 2,2,4-trimethylpentane.

items: Longest chain = parent; number from the end nearest a substituent; substituents first with numbers, alphabetical (ignore di, tri); same carbon: number twice; identical groups: di, tri; equal chains: more substituents; equal branch distance: lower number at first difference.
